title: Array Operations and What They Cost
quickIdea: Reading or writing one cell is O(1); inserting or deleting in the middle is O(n), because every later element has to move one slot.
remember: Access by index: O(1), because the address formula is arithmetic.
Search: O(n) in an unsorted array; O(log n) by binary search in a sorted array.
Insert at index k of an array holding n elements: n - k elements shift right, so the worst case (k = 0) is n moves and the average over the n + 1 insertion positions is n/2.
Delete at index k of an array holding n elements: n - 1 - k elements shift left; deleting the last element moves nothing.
A dynamic array that doubles its capacity when full copies 1 + 2 + 4 + ... + n/2 = n - 1 elements over n appends, so append is O(1) amortised but O(n) in the worst single call.
The size of a plain C array is fixed at declaration; growing it means allocating a new block and copying.

example.prompt: An array holds 10 elements. How many element moves does one insertion take at the front, at the back, and on average?
example.work: Inserting at index 0 shifts all 10 elements: 10 moves. Inserting at index 10 (after the last element) shifts nothing: 0 moves. The 11 possible positions need 10, 9, 8, ..., 1, 0 moves, whose sum is 55, and 55 / 11 = 5 = n/2.
example.answer: 10 moves at the front, 0 at the back, 5 on average.

gateAngle: GATE asks this cost model inside trace questions rather than as a definition: a loop that inserts at the front of an array n times costs Theta(n^2), while the same loop appending at the end costs Theta(n). Reading a cost off the code is faster than recalling a table.

variations.label: ORIGINAL PYQ-STYLE QUESTION
variations.question: A dynamic array starts with capacity 1 and doubles whenever it is full. Starting empty, how many element copies do 8 appends cause in total, and what is the final capacity?
variations.why: Copies happen only when the array is full: 1 copy at the 2nd append, 2 at the 3rd, 4 at the 5th, and none afterwards, so 1 + 2 + 4 = 7 = n - 1 for n = 8. This is the amortised-O(1) argument in one line.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: An array of n elements is sorted. Is deleting its smallest element O(1) because the element's address is known?
variations.why: Knowing where the element sits does not remove the shifting: deleting index 0 moves the other n - 1 elements left to keep the block contiguous. Random access is O(1); deletion is not.

trap.what: Believing that O(1) random access makes every array operation O(1).
trap.why: The address formula only locates a cell. Keeping the array contiguous after an insert or delete is the expensive part, and that cost is paid in moves, not in lookups.
trap.counterexample: Deleting the first of 1,000,000 elements takes 999,999 moves even though its address is computed instantly. Only deleting the last element is O(1).

check.question: An array holds n = 10 elements. How many element moves does deleting the element at index 0 take?
check.explanation: The 9 elements after it each shift one slot left, so the count is n - 1 - k with k = 0, which is 9. Deleting the last element (k = 9) would take 0 moves.
